tier_reason: COMPARISON.md times pure-rand against native Math.random (Node 16.19.1, Xorshift128+) and the seedrandom, faker, chance and random-js generators. The benchmark code is public (perf/compare.cjs, pinned at commit 556ec331, tinybench, 1,000 iterations of a 1,000,000-item Fisher-Yates shuffle). The runtime version (Node 16.19.1, default flags) and the CPU (Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL @ 2.60GHz, GitHub Actions runner) are stated, so A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Node 16.19.1 (V8 JIT, default flags), pure-rand 6.0.0; benchmark script perf/compare.cjs (permalinked from COMPARISON.md at commit 556ec331) uses tinybench with 1,000 iterations and about 50 warmup iterations
corrections.caveats: JavaScript only, not usable from C++. Measured on shared GitHub Actions runners (noisy), with old versions (pure-rand 6.0.0, Node 16). The workload is a Fisher-Yates shuffle, so it measures range reduction as well as the generator. The non-uniform pure-rand rows call the mutating unsafeNext() API rather than the pure next() API the library is named for. The native Math.random baseline appears only in the non-uniform section; the uniform section compares only against random-js. COMPARISON.md's prose calls the non-uniform section 'known to be slower' (rejection resampling), which describes the uniform section; the tables themselves are consistent. Run by the project author. The 'Congruential' generator (congruential32 in the code) is listed as 1.1x faster than the recommended Xoroshiro128+ in the non-uniform table.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches COMPARISON.md exactly. Metadata confirmed on github.com: MIT, 117 stars, 5 forks, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-07-10 (active). Scope flag: TypeScript/JavaScript library, kept as a non-C++ entry like other wave 8 non-C++ RNG entries.

tier_reason: The README benchmark block comes from public benchmark code (xorshift_test.go, which includes BenchmarkRandSource on math/rand.NewSource Int63 and BenchmarkRand on rand.New(...).ExpFloat64). It states the toolchain and flags (Go 1.14, go test -bench=., defaults) and the CPU (i7-3840QM, Fedora 31, Linux 5.6.9), so A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Raw source ns/op: math/rand BenchmarkRandSource 4.93 versus XorShift128Plus 2.42, XorShift1024Star 2.40, Xoroshiro128Plus 2.66, Xoroshiro256PlusPlus 3.86, Xoroshiro256StarStar 3.93, Xoroshiro512Plus 6.15, Xoroshiro512StarStar 6.34, SplitMix64 1.61. Wrapped in rand.Rand (ExpFloat64): BenchmarkRand 10.2 versus XorShift128Plus 8.42, Xoroshiro128Plus 8.10, SplitMix64 8.66, but Xoroshiro256PlusPlus and Xoroshiro256StarStar 11.7, XorShift1024Star 9.61, Xoroshiro512Plus 13.2 and Xoroshiro512StarStar 13.6. Raw speedup is about 2.0x for XorShift128Plus and 3.1x for SplitMix64; once wrapped it is only about 1.2x, and the 256- and 512-bit-state xoroshiro variants are slower than math/rand (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Go package, not callable from C++. Numbers are from 2020 on a 2012-era laptop CPU with Go 1.14, run by the repo author. The raw rows are asymmetric: the generators' Uint64() is called on the concrete type returned by NewSource (static dispatch, inlinable), while the baseline calls Int63() through the rand.Source interface (dynamic dispatch), so part of the raw 2-3x gap is call overhead. The wrapped rows go through rand.Rand on both sides and show only about 1.2x, with the 256/512-bit-state variants slower than math/rand. The baseline is Go's default math/rand source, not a C++ standard facility. Go's standard library has since added math/rand/v2 (PCG, ChaCha8), so the gap against current Go is likely smaller (background knowledge, not tested).

notes: All quoted ns/op values match the README; the record omitted that several wrapped variants lose to math/rand, which I added. Metadata confirmed on github.com and the LICENSE file: MIT, 16 stars, 1 fork, not a fork or archived, last commit 2020-05-02 (abandoned).

corrections.caveats: Independent but casual single-author benchmark gist: code, compiler and GCC flags are public, but no CPU model is stated and MSVC flags are not given. Pcg32 returns 32 bits per call while the Romu 64-bit variants return 64, so GiB/s mixes output widths. No std::mt19937 or other std:: engine row. Under MSVC the ranking changes: Wyrand 12.81 GiB/s beats RomuDuoJr 11.53. The gist carries no license of its own: the Romu code credits Mark A. Overton (romu-random.org, license not confirmed), the Wyrand code is marked Unlicense and the xoroshiro128+ code credits Blackman and Vigna. Last gist activity 2022-11-24.
